justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a mildly bullish baseline assumption across all three horizons, with prices drifting slightly higher from a presumed current level around 208–209. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 209.5 essentially reflects mean-reversion tendencies and the assumption that no major overnight catalyst has materialized, so the price stays close to its recent anchor. At the one-week horizon, the modest uptick to 210.5 incorporates a slight positive drift assumption consistent with the broader trend, while acknowledging that short-term noise could easily dominate. At the one-month horizon, the estimate of 212 reflects a continuation of that gentle upward drift, compounded over a longer period, but tempered by the recognition that mean-reverting forces, valuation constraints, or macro headwinds could limit gains.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated to reflect typical realized volatility scaling with the square root of time. At one day, the 90% interval of roughly plus or minus 5–5.5 points around the estimate reflects normal intraday-to-overnight price ranges for the asset in question. At one week, the interval widens to roughly plus or minus 10–10.5 points, consistent with weekly volatility. At one month, the interval expands further to roughly plus or minus 19 points, capturing the compounding uncertainty over a four-week window. These widths implicitly assume a relatively stable volatility regime without an imminent vol shock.

The primary sources of uncertainty include macroeconomic data releases such as inflation prints, employment reports, or central bank communications that could cause sharp repricing across a wide range of assets. Earnings announcements, geopolitical developments, or sudden shifts in risk appetite could also drive outcomes well outside these intervals. Liquidity conditions matter too — thin markets can amplify moves beyond what historical volatility would suggest.

The most significant tail risks that could push outcomes outside my stated intervals include a surprise policy shift from a major central bank, an unexpected geopolitical escalation, or a credit or liquidity event that triggers correlated selling. On the upside, a stronger-than-expected growth signal or a dovish policy pivot could push prices well above 231 at the one-month horizon. On the downside, a risk-off episode or disappointing fundamental news could easily breach the lower bound of 193. These intervals are probabilistic statements, not hard limits, and the actual tails of the distribution are always fatter than any symmetric Gaussian approximation implies.
